t: A ball sits still. Then it moves. What happened in between?
A ball is at rest. Then it is moving. Something changed its speed — what?
A stationary ball begins to move. A moving ball comes to rest. Both involve a change in speed.
An object at rest acquires velocity; a moving object loses it. Both are changes in the rate of change of position.
sub: Its speed changed. That change has a name.
Speed does not just appear. It changes — and the rate of that change is a thing.
The rate at which speed changes is called acceleration.
The time derivative of velocity is acceleration — a vector quantity, m/s².

question: The ball is slowing down because of friction. Is it accelerating?
A ball slows down because of friction. Is it accelerating?
A rolling ball's speed decreases due to friction. Is it accelerating?
An object decelerates due to kinetic friction. Is its acceleration nonzero?
options: Yes, slowing down is accelerating — just in the opposite direction
No, accelerating only means speeding up
No, friction is not a real acceleration
stages.outcome: Yes, slowing down is accelerating — just in the opposite direction
note: This one surprises people. Guess what you think, then check.
Predict before checking. The answer is the opposite of what most people expect.
Form a hypothesis. Deceleration is a kind of acceleration — predict which.
Predict: is deceleration a subset of acceleration, or a distinct phenomenon?

t: Push the ball, then let friction slow it. Watch the speed arrow shrink.
Launch the ball and watch friction slow it. The speed arrow shrinks — that is acceleration, pointing backwards.
goal: Watch the speed arrow shrink as friction slows the ball. That shrinking is acceleration.
Observe the velocity arrow decreasing in magnitude. That rate of decrease is acceleration.

t: Find a push and friction where the ball speeds up, then slows down. Both are acceleration.
Configure push and friction so the ball accelerates then decelerates. Both phases involve nonzero acceleration — identify the direction in each.
goal: Reach the goal. The ball sped up, then slowed down — both are acceleration.
Reach the goal. The velocity increased then decreased; acceleration was positive then negative.

t: When speed changes — faster or slower — that is called acceleration.
A change in speed is called acceleration. Speeding up and slowing down are both acceleration.
Acceleration is how fast speed changes. It is measured in metres per second per second (m/s²).
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = Δv/Δt. A vector, m/s². Deceleration is acceleration antiparallel to velocity.
sub: Speeding up is acceleration forward. Slowing down is acceleration backward.
More push means more acceleration. More friction means acceleration backward (slowing).
Friction causes acceleration opposite to motion. The sign of acceleration relative to velocity determines speed-up vs slow-down.
a = F_net/m by Newton's second law. Friction produces a negative acceleration; the applied force, a positive one.

t: When a car brakes, it is accelerating backward. The faster it was going, the longer that takes.
A braking car is accelerating backwards. The faster it was going, the longer it takes to stop.
Braking is deceleration. At 70 mph a car takes about 96 m to stop; at 30 mph, about 14 m. The relationship is quadratic.
Braking distance scales as v²/(2a). The quadratic dependence on initial speed is why urban speed limits save lives disproportionately.

q: A ball is slowing down. Is it accelerating?
A rolling ball's speed is decreasing. Is it accelerating?
An object's speed is decreasing. Is its acceleration nonzero?
An object decelerates. Is a nonzero?
options: Yes — slowing down is acceleration in the opposite direction
No, acceleration only means speeding up
why: Acceleration is any change in speed. Slowing down is acceleration pointing against the motion — the friction force pushes it backward.
Acceleration is a change in velocity, including decreases. Friction produces acceleration opposite to motion, which slows the ball.
a = Δv/Δt. If v decreases, Δv is negative, so a is negative (opposite to motion). Deceleration is acceleration with sign reversed.
Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity. Any change in velocity's magnitude or direction constitutes acceleration; deceleration is the case where a · v < 0.

q: You push a ball. It speeds up. Where is the acceleration pointing?
A ball speeds up when you push it. Which way does the acceleration point?
An object's speed increases under a push. What is the direction of its acceleration?
Under an applied force, an object's speed increases. What is the sign of a relative to v?
options: Forward — the same way it is moving
why: The push is forward, so the acceleration is forward. The ball speeds up because the acceleration points the same way it is moving.
Acceleration points in the direction of the net force. The push is forward, so acceleration is forward — and speed increases.
a = F_net/m. The applied force is forward, so a is forward. When a is parallel to v, speed increases.
By Newton's second law, a is parallel to F_net. When a · v > 0, speed increases; the applied force provides the parallel component.
